blocks.x: “Physical self-awareness is the first step in releasing the tyranny of the past.” ~ Bessel van der Kolk
For years, I thought my anxiety was a character flaw. I thought I could think my way through it. Reason with myself long enough, and I’d finally get to the other side of it. I never did.

Every time I thought I had made peace with it, something small would happen, and I’d be right back in that place. Heart racing. Hands shaking. Anticipating a fallout in something that hadn’t even happened yet.

In my previous marriage, I learned to read a room before I even understood I was reading it. I could tell from the sound of a door closing how the night was going to play out. I walked on eggshells for years.

My body knew things my mind hadn’t caught up to yet. I’d feel my chest tighten and my stomach drop, and I’d start smoothing things over before I even knew what I was smoothing over. I called it being “sensitive” or “too much.” I never once called it what it actually was.

When I finally left that marriage, I thought the anxiety would leave with it. It didn’t. Years later, in situations that weren’t dangerous at all, I’d still feel that same tightness in my chest. A raised voice in another room. A delayed text back. Someone going quiet during an argument. My body would react like I was in danger even when I wasn’t.
My mind would spend hours afterward trying to talk myself down from something it hadn’t fully understood in the first place.
I didn’t understand what was actually happening until I started training as a health counselor and studying attachment theory.

My anxiety was a nervous system that had learned a long time ago that danger could show up without warning. It built a whole set of reactions to keep me safe. Reactions that fired on their own long before my conscious thoughts ever got a vote.

That’s what anxious attachment looks like from the inside. A nervous system that learned early that connection could disappear without warning, so it stays braced for loss even when nothing’s actually wrong.

This is what nervous system dysregulation looks like day to day. A body that learned, at some point, to treat ordinary stress like a real threat. It keeps sounding the alarm until something teaches it otherwise.
This is the part that took me the longest to understand. No amount of reasoning with myself touched it. That reaction lived somewhere older and faster than the reasoning part of my brain.
A part of me that had learned its lessons through repetition, emotion, and the body itself, long before I had words for any of it.

A nervous system responds to repetition, emotion, and physiology. That’s how change actually happens and new neuropathways get formed—by working a new pattern into the body the same way the old one got there.
The shift that changed everything for me started very small. I started paying attention to the reaction while it was happening.

Even now, in a relationship where I’m safe and loved, I sometimes catch it. My partner goes quiet for a few minutes, and my chest tightens before I can stop it. The old questions surface: Is he mad? Did I do something? My body braces for impact that isn’t coming.

But now I notice it. Right as my chest tightens, right as my shoulders creep up toward my ears, I put my hand on my chest and breathe deeply until it softens. I name what my body is actually doing. My chest is tight. My shoulders are up around my ears. I’m holding my breath. That’s all.
Just naming it, staying with it, letting it move through me. I remind myself that silence doesn’t mean what it used to mean. I stay in the present moment instead of disappearing into old stories.
Over time—and it did take time—that pause grew. The gap between the trigger and my reaction went from nothing to a second. Then a few seconds. Then long enough that I could choose what happened next.

I started responding to what was actually happening in front of me, paying attention to the present moment on its own terms. That gap is where my life changed. Slowly, in all the small ordinary moments where I used to disappear into old patterns without even noticing I’d left, it began to shift.

If you’ve spent years feeling like your anxiety is some kind of personal failing or something you should’ve fixed by now through sheer willpower or enough therapy or enough journaling, I want you to hear this. Your body is doing exactly what it learned to do to keep you safe, and it’s still doing that job today. Even in situations where you’re not in danger anymore.

Healing starts in the body, with noticing what’s happening there before your mind even catches up to explain it. Regulating your nervous system can start right where you are, with something as simple as noticing one sensation and staying with it a few seconds longer than usual.
Here’s what I’ve learned about working with a nervous system.
First, notice before you narrate.

The instant something happens in your body, your mind wants to jump in with a story about what it means. Before you get to the story, just notice the sensation itself. The tight chest. The shallow breath. The urge to apologize or explain or disappear. Notice it the way you’d notice weather moving across the sky, without deciding yet what it means about you.

Let’s say someone you love goes quiet. Before you ask what’s wrong or start replaying the last hour looking for what you did, pause. Put your hand somewhere grounding—your chest, your belly, your thigh. Notice what’s happening in your body right now. Name it without explaining it. Tight chest. Shallow breath. Urge to fix. That’s the first step.
Second, breathe through it before you decide what to do next.

Anxiety wants you to act immediately. Fix it. Explain it. Smooth it over. Most of the time, there’s no real emergency requiring that speed. A few slow breaths won’t cost you anything, and they give your body enough time to remember it’s not actually under attack.

In that same moment, with the quiet partner and the tightening chest, try this: Breathe in for four counts. Out for six. Let your exhale be longer than your inhale. Do it two or three times before you say or do anything. You’re not ignoring the situation. You’re giving your body a chance to come back online before you respond from a place that isn’t actually about what’s happening right now.
Third, expect this to take repetition.

The pattern took years to build, and it won’t undo itself the first time you try something new. Every time you pause before reacting, even for one extra second, you’re teaching your nervous system something it didn’t know before. That adds up slowly. Then one day you realize the gap that used to be a fraction of a second is now long enough to actually live in.

This shift is available to you no matter where you’re starting from. Even if therapy hasn’t touched it yet. Even if you’ve read every book and tried every technique and still find yourself reacting the same old way.

The body holds the pattern, and the body can learn a new one. It happens through paying attention, gently and consistently, until your nervous system finally believes what your mind’s known for a while now. That you’re safe and that you get to decide what happens next.

I still catch old patterns sometimes. A voice raised in another room can still make my chest tighten for half a second before I remember where I actually am. The difference now is I notice it. I breathe through it. I get to choose what happens next, and so do you.
